contentBeforeToc:
One store with Shopify Markets can easily handle most international and multi-brand needs quite well. But that doesn’t happen all the time. Because there can be some situations that genuinely call for separate stores, and choosing wrong in either direction would make you end up with real operational pain.

But the question is: how would you make that call? To understand that phenomenon, let’s explore…
contentAfterToc:
The Default: One Store, Multiple Markets

For most brands selling internationally, one Shopify store with Markets is the cleaner approach. Currencies, languages, domains, and pricing all adjust per region from a single back end, single inventory, single admin, single source of truth. This is almost always simpler to manage than running parallel stores.

When Multiple Stores Actually Make Sense

  • Entirely different catalogs. If you’re running distinct brands with different products, not just different pricing on the same catalog, separate stores keep each brand’s inventory, merchandising, and identity genuinely independent.
  • Separate accounting entities. If each region or brand needs to operate as its own legal or financial entity, with distinct reporting and settlement, a single shared store can complicate that separation.
  • B2B and B2C run as fundamentally different businesses. Running both on one system, one inventory, one customer experience, can create real operational chaos as each side scales. Some brands are better served splitting them into separate storefronts entirely.
  • A market needs a genuinely distinct local presence. Not just a translated version of your main store by a Shopify Development agency or by yourself, but a market where branding, product mix, or positioning needs to diverge meaningfully from your primary storefront.

The Trade-Offs of Going Multi-Store

  • Separate inventories. Each store manages stock independently, which gives you real separation, but also means no shared visibility unless you build that connection yourself.
  • Duplicated admin work. Settings, apps, and configurations often need to be replicated across each store rather than managed once.
  • Higher technical overhead. Multiple stores typically mean more complex data syncing, more surface area for integrations, and more places things can drift out of sync.
  • Cost. On Shopify Plus, expansion stores are included in the base plan, up to 9, each fully independent with its own domain, catalog, and pricing. Outside that structure, running multiple full stores can mean effectively paying for multiple subscriptions.

A Simple Way to Decide

  • Same brand, same products, different regions? Use one store with Markets.
  • Different brands, different catalogs, or separate legal entities? Multi-store is likely the right call.
  • B2B and B2C growing into very different operational needs? Worth seriously evaluating separate storefronts.
  • Just want a “more local feel” without real catalog or brand differences? Markets’ localization tools usually deliver this without the overhead of a second store.

What This Looks Like on Shopify Plus

If Shopify multi-store is the right answer, Shopify Plus’s expansion stores are built for exactly this: each operates as a fully independent storefront, with its own domain, products, pricing, and branding, without needing to purchase or manage entirely separate subscriptions.

This is typically the structure growing brands land on once they’ve confirmed multi-store is genuinely necessary, not just a reflexive choice.

The Bottom Line

Multi-store isn’t a sign of a more sophisticated setup; it’s a specific answer to a specific problem: genuinely separate catalogs, entities, or business models. If your situation is really about reaching customers in more places with the same brand and products, Markets almost always does the job with far less operational complexity.

Haven’t ruled out a single-store approach yet?
